questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish regulation of enzyme amount from regulation of enzyme activity
questions.stem: In the first week of the coral tank log, the marine biologist notes that a gene can be controlled in two different ways. Which statement about regulation by amount versus activity is correct?

options.text: Control can act by changing how much protein is made or how active the protein already present is.
Control can act only by changing how much protein is made, because activity cannot be altered after synthesis.
options.misconception: believes activity is fixed once a protein is made

options.text: Control can act only by switching existing proteins off, since new protein can never be made on demand.
options.misconception: claims new protein cannot be made on demand

options.text: Control works by changing the DNA sequence so that a different protein is produced instead.

questions.explanation: A cell can regulate a gene by making more or less protein, or by activating or inhibiting the protein it already has. Claiming activity is fixed once a protein exists misdescribes the two routes.
questions.hint: Ask what is being changed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: A Factor Looping DNA to a Promoter
questions.learningObjective: Interpret expression data across distances between a binding site and a promoter
questions.stem: The 14 February entry records expression for four constructs, each with the factor's site moved further from the promoter: 100 units at 200 base pairs, 78 at 800, 31 at 3000 and 12 at 12000. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The factor's effect is the same at every distance, so the site position cannot matter for expression.
The factor can only work within 800 base pairs, because no expression was measured beyond that point.
The factor's effect depends on how close its site is to the promoter, and it fades as distance grows.
The factor's binding site must lie inside the gene itself, since it was present in every construct.
options.misconception: requires the site inside the gene

questions.explanation: Expression falls steadily as the site is moved away, so the factor acts through a contact favoured by short distances rather than at a fixed range. Claiming a strict cutoff goes beyond the data.
questions.hint: Look at the trend across the four constructs.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Wrapping DNA and Adding an Acetyl Tag
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the fold change in transcription after DNA is given an acetyl tag
questions.stem: The 3 March entry records that a gene's transcript count was 50 in untreated tank cells and 350 after the DNA around it was wrapped with proteins carrying an added acetyl tag. By what factor did transcription increase?
questions.explanation: The transcript count rose from 50 to 350, so the factor is 350 / 50 = 7. Subtracting the two counts gives 300, which is the difference rather than the factor that was asked for.
questions.hint: Divide the larger count by the smaller.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Needing Several Factors at Once
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a promoter may require several factors to be present together
questions.stem: During a quiet afternoon the marine biologist writes about a promoter that switches on only when three separate factors are present together. Explain why a promoter might require several factors at the same time.

answer.exemplar: Requiring several factors makes a promoter sensitive to a particular combination of conditions, so the gene is switched on only when all the right signals are present at once and stays off if any one of them is missing. This is how a cell separates responses that would otherwise look identical, such as switching on a repair pathway only when damage and low growth occur together. It also lets the cell change the response by changing the amount of one factor rather than rewriting the gene.

questions.explanation: Requiring several factors makes the gene respond to a combination of conditions, so it is switched on only when all are present. Treating each factor as an independent switch misses the point.
questions.hint: Think about what a combination of inputs detects.

questions.stem: The 20 April page draws a bar chart with two bars for each condition: for plain seawater 20 units of message and 30 units of protein, for warmed seawater 60 units of message and 35 units of protein. What does the chart show?

options.text: That warming raised both the message and the protein by the same amount, so the response is direct.
That warming raised the message sharply but the protein hardly, so translation is being held back.
That the protein amounts were measured wrongly, since they changed so little between conditions.
That warming reduced the message and the protein, since the bars for warmed seawater are shorter.

questions.explanation: The message rises sixfold while the protein hardly moves, so something downstream of transcription is limiting the protein. Reading the protein change as an error contradicts the chart.
questions.hint: Compare the two sets of bars.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Where and Everywhere a Gene Is Read
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that a gene must be read everywhere it is present
questions.stem: A dive volunteer claims that a gene found in the brain and the gills of a fish must be switched on in both places at the same time, because the gene is present in every cell. Identify what is wrong with this reasoning.

options.text: The error is that genes are only present in the cells where they are switched on.
The error is that a gene can only be read in one tissue over the life of the organism.
options.misconception: claims a gene works in one tissue only

options.text: The error is that the same gene can be present everywhere while being read only where its control DNA allows.
The error is that the brain and the gills of a fish cannot both contain the same gene.
options.misconception: denies that a gene is in every cell

questions.explanation: Every cell carries the same genes, but control sequences decide where a gene is read, so a gene can be active in the gills and silent in the brain. Claiming it exists only where it works misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask where the control sequences act.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: A Small RNA Switching Messages Off
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment showing that a small RNA reduces a target message
questions.stem: The 5 June page asks how the small RNA that silences a message could be tested. Describe an experiment showing that a small RNA reduces the amount of a target message.

answer.exemplar: Introduce into the tank cells a construct that produces the target message together with either the candidate small RNA or an unrelated small RNA of similar size as a control, and measure the amount of the message in each culture at several time points by a reverse transcriptase reaction. If the target message falls faster and ends lower in the cultures with the candidate RNA while the control RNA has no effect, the silencing is specific to that small RNA, and adding back a version unable to pair with the message should restore the message level.

questions.explanation: An unrelated small RNA of similar size controls for a general effect on stability, and a time course shows faster loss of the target message. A non-pairing version tests if pairing matters.
questions.hint: You need a control small RNA of similar size.

questions.topic: Mutation: A Change That Alters No Amino Acid
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a DNA change can leave the protein unchanged
questions.stem: The 12 July entry notes a DNA change in a gene that leaves the protein exactly the same. Which statement about such a change is correct?

options.text: The change must have altered the protein, because DNA and protein use the same sequence of bases.
options.misconception: claims DNA and protein share base sequences

options.text: The change can only be harmless if it occurred in a part of the gene that is never copied.
options.misconception: claims the change must be untranscribed

options.text: The change is always harmful, since any difference in DNA must change the protein.
options.misconception: claims all DNA changes alter protein

options.text: The change may be silent, for example when a codon is altered but still specifies the same amino acid.

questions.explanation: Some codon changes still specify the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged and the change may be harmless. Claiming every DNA change alters the protein overlooks silent changes.
questions.hint: Ask what a codon change can leave unchanged.

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity

questions.stem: The 19 September page tabulates an enzyme in two tank conditions: in the cool tank 200 units of enzyme with a rate of 5 per minute, and in the warm tank 200 units of enzyme with a rate of 20 per minute. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: The warm tank has more enzyme, since the rate is four times higher there.
The cool tank has a defective gene, since its enzyme cannot work at all.
Both tanks hold the same enzyme amount, so the temperature acts on the enzyme's activity.
The enzyme is inactive in the warm tank, since heat is known to denature enzymes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Wrapping DNA and Adding an Acetyl Tag
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an acetyl tag loosens DNA for copying
questions.stem: The 14 August page asks why wrapping DNA around proteins and adding an acetyl group to those proteins can increase transcription. Explain how that change loosens the DNA for copying.

answer.exemplar: DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form chromatin, and that wrapping holds the DNA tightly and limits access for copying. Adding an acetyl group to a histone neutralises a charge on its tail, which loosens the grip on the wrapped DNA and lets copying factors reach the promoter. The histones also carry marks that recruit reader proteins, so acetylation can bring in activators as well as open the DNA, and the mark can be removed again to close the region down.

questions.explanation: Wrapped DNA is harder to reach, and an acetyl group weakens that grip and draws in activators, so transcription rises. Claiming the tag changes the DNA sequence misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Think about how the DNA is held shut.

That each factor independently starts its own transcript from the same promoter.

options.text: That the three factors act one after another in a fixed sequence along the DNA.
That the three factors compete with one another for the same binding site on the DNA.

questions.explanation: Three arrows converging on one promoter with one arrow leaving for a transcript shows a gene needing all three factors before it is copied. Reading the factors as competitors misreads the lines.
questions.hint: Notice that all the arrows meet.

questions.topic: Gene Expression: Message Level versus Protein Level
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that message level fixes protein level
questions.stem: The 4 February entry claims that if a gene's messenger RNA level does not change, then the level of its protein cannot change either. Identify what is wrong with this claim.

options.text: The claim is wrong because messenger RNA levels are never measured in a living cell.
The claim is wrong because protein levels are always much higher than messenger RNA levels.
The claim is wrong because proteins are made only when the messenger RNA is copied.
The claim is wrong because translation can be altered later, so protein can change while the RNA stays steady.

questions.explanation: Protein levels depend on translation efficiency and on how long the protein lasts, so protein can change while the message stays steady. Claiming the two must move together misstates the process.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Where and Everywhere a Gene Is Read
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment comparing one gene's reading in two tissues
questions.stem: The 11 November page asks how it could be shown that one gene is read in the gills but not in the brain of the same fish. Describe the experiment.

answer.exemplar: Take matched samples of gill and brain tissue from the same animals, isolate the messenger RNA from each and measure the amount of the target message with a reverse transcriptase reaction, alongside a control message from a gene that is switched on in every tissue. If the target message is abundant in the gill and absent from the brain while the control message is present in both, the gene is read in one tissue and not the other, which the identical DNA in every cell makes possible.

questions.explanation: Measuring the same message in gill and brain tissue, with a broadly active gene as a control, shows whether the gene is read in one tissue only. Comparing different animals would confound the result.
questions.hint: Compare two tissues from the same animal.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Message Level versus Protein Level
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment measuring message and protein in the same cells
questions.stem: The 25 May page asks how a difference between message level and protein level could be demonstrated. Describe an experiment measuring both in the same cells.

answer.exemplar: Take matched tank cultures, treat one with whatever changes the gene's regulation, and leave the other untreated, then measure the amount of the target messenger RNA in each by a reverse transcriptase reaction and the amount of the corresponding protein by an antibody assay or a gel. questions.explanation: Measuring message and protein in the same treated and untreated cultures shows whether the two move together, and a control gene shows if the change is specific. Protein alone is not enough.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Mutation: A Change That Alters No Amino Acid
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a silent change arises and what it can still affect
questions.stem: The 3 December page asks how a DNA change can leave a protein untouched, and what such a change can still do. Explain how a silent change occurs and what it can affect.

answer.exemplar: Several different codons can specify the same amino acid, so a change in the third base of a codon can swap one synonym for another and leave the protein exactly as it was. Such a change is often harmless for the protein, but it can still alter how often a message is made, how it is translated, or how stable it is, because those depend on the sequence of the message rather than on the amino acids. It can also act as a marker in the study of inherited variation.

questions.explanation: Several codons specify the same amino acid, so some changes leave the protein identical while still altering the message. Calling every change harmful overlooks silent changes.
questions.hint: Think about redundancy in the code.

questions.stem: The 15 August page asks how it could be shown that a promoter really needs all three of its factors. Describe the experiment.

answer.exemplar: Build three versions of a construct that differ only in which of the three factors is present, keeping the promoter and the reporter sequence identical, and measure the reporter output in each. Removing the factors one at a time, rather than all together, shows which ones matter and whether any one of them can partly replace another.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Where and Everywhere a Gene Is Read
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the same gene can be read in one tissue and not another
questions.stem: During a night dive the biologist writes that a gene can be present in every cell of a fish but switched on in only some of them. Explain how the same DNA can be read in one tissue and not another.

answer.exemplar: Every cell of the fish carries the same DNA, so the difference between tissues lies in the control DNA beside each gene and in the factors each tissue contains. A region that is wrapped tightly and marked in one tissue may stay closed, while in another the same region is opened and the needed factors are present, so the gene is copied into messenger RNA. The gene itself is identical in both tissues; only the signals that decide when it is read differ.

questions.explanation: Tissues differ in the control DNA around genes and in the factors they contain, so a gene can be copied in one tissue and closed in another. Claiming the DNA differs between tissues is wrong.
questions.hint: Think about what surrounds the gene.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a small regulatory RNA and describe its role
questions.stem: The 2 October entry introduces the short regulatory RNA found in the tank cells. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: It is a messenger RNA fragment that is read to make a small protein.
It is a long RNA that carries the message from the nucleus for translation.
options.misconception: confuses it with a messenger RNA

options.text: It is a protein that binds the DNA and stops the gene being copied.
options.misconception: calls the small RNA a protein

options.text: It is a short RNA that guides a protein complex to a matching message so it is removed or blocked.

questions.explanation: A short regulatory RNA pairs with a complementary target and recruits a protein complex that removes the message or stops it being read. Calling it a fragment or a protein confuses it.
questions.hint: Ask what it pairs with.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Mutation: A Change That Alters No Amino Acid
questions.learningObjective: Explain what can differ when the protein sequence does not
questions.stem: The 13 May entry records a DNA change in a coding region that leaves the protein sequence exactly the same, and asks what can still differ. Which statement fits?

options.text: Nothing can differ, because the protein sequence is all that a gene produces.
options.misconception: ignores the message and other outputs

options.text: Only the location of the gene on the DNA can differ, since the sequence of the gene is fixed.
The sequence of the messenger RNA can differ even though the protein sequence is unchanged.
The number of copies of the gene must differ, since a silent change can add or remove copies.

questions.explanation: Several codons specify the same amino acid, so a change can leave the protein identical while altering the message. Claiming the message cannot differ misreads a single base substitution.
questions.hint: Ask what the protein does not record.

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity

questions.stem: The 9 April entry notes that a tank holds 600 units of an enzyme, each working at 3 units of product per minute, and that a second tank holds the same enzyme at one third of that activity. How many units of product per minute does the second tank make?
questions.explanation: The first tank makes 600 x 3 = 1800 units of product a minute, and the second has one third of that activity per molecule, so it makes 600 x 1 = 600 units. The change is in activity, not amount.
questions.hint: Multiply the amount by the rate.

That the factor must unhook from the DNA for the gene to be switched on.

That the promoter is copied into the regulatory sequence so the loop can be closed.

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Wrapping DNA and Adding an Acetyl Tag
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that an acetyl tag alters the DNA sequence
questions.stem: The 5 January entry claims that adding an acetyl tag to the proteins around DNA adds an acetyl group to the DNA sequence itself, so the gene's code changes. Identify what is wrong with this claim.

options.text: The error is that acetyl groups can only be added to proteins in the cytoplasm.
The error is that the tag is added to the proteins, not to the DNA bases, so the gene's sequence is unchanged.
The error is that no chemical group can change how tightly DNA is held.
The error is that an acetyl tag always removes the DNA from the chromosome.

questions.explanation: The tag is carried on the proteins that hold the DNA, so the bases are untouched and the gene's sequence is unchanged. Claiming the tag alters the code misdescribes the modification.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Needing Several Factors at Once
questions.learningObjective: State what a promoter requiring three factors allows a cell to do
questions.stem: The 10 March entry describes a promoter that is inactive unless three factors are present. Which statement best describes what that arrangement allows?

options.text: It allows the gene to be switched on at any time, since three factors are easier to gather.
It allows the gene to be switched on by any one of the factors acting alone.
It allows the protein made from the gene to work without any of the three factors.
It allows the cell to read the gene only when all three signals are present at once, which is precise control.

questions.explanation: Requiring all three factors means the gene is read only when that exact combination of signals is present. Treating the factors as individually sufficient misses the point.
questions.hint: Think about what the combination detects.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Message Level versus Protein Level
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment comparing message and protein in one culture
questions.stem: The 22 July page asks how the message level and the protein level could be compared in the same tank cells. Describe the experiment.

answer.exemplar: Take one culture of tank cells and measure two things from it: the amount of the target messenger RNA by a reverse transcriptase reaction, and the amount of the corresponding protein with an antibody that recognises it or by running a sample on a gel and comparing band intensities with a standard. Splitting the culture into untreated and treated halves and repeating both measurements in each shows whether the two levels moved together, and any difference in band intensity can be checked against the standard.

questions.explanation: Measuring message and protein in matched halves of one culture shows whether the two respond alike, and a standard makes the amounts comparable. Measuring one alone proves nothing.
questions.hint: Measure both in matched halves.

The gene is absent from the brain, since only 3 units of message were found there.

questions.explanation: The gill shows most message, muscle and liver clear amounts, and the brain almost none, so the gene is read at different levels in several tissues. A low amount means weak reading.

options.text: That every change in a codon changes the amino acid, so no change is silent.
That the third base of a codon has no effect at all on the amino acid.
options.misconception: claims the third base never matters

options.text: That different codons can give the same amino acid, so some changes leave the protein the same.
That glycine and valine are made from the same base sequence by different enzymes.

questions.explanation: Two different codons giving the same amino acid is what makes a third base change silent, so the protein can be identical while the message differs. Not every change alters the protein.

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that higher activity proves more copying of the gene
questions.stem: The 12 September log claims that the fourfold rise in enzyme activity in the warmed tank proves the gene was copied four times more often. Identify what is wrong with this claim.

options.text: The error is that genes cannot be copied more often at all, since each is copied once per cell.
options.misconception: claims genes are copied once only

options.text: The error is that the same amount of enzyme can work faster, so activity can rise without more copying.
The error is that the measurement of activity was made on the wrong tank.
The error is that activity can only fall as temperature rises, because heat denatures protein.

questions.explanation: Activity can rise because the same enzyme molecules work faster, so a fourfold rise in rate does not show more copying. Assuming heat always denatures enzymes ignores that.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: A Factor Looping DNA to a Promoter
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a distant regulatory site can influence a promoter
questions.stem: The 17 January entry asks why a regulatory site can control a gene that lies far away along the DNA. Explain how a distant site can influence a promoter.

answer.exemplar: The DNA is flexible enough to fold so that a regulatory site and a distant promoter end up side by side, and a factor bound at the site can then touch the machinery at the promoter, either helping or blocking it. Because folding brings the two together more often when they are close together, the effect of a distant site falls as the gap grows. The same folding lets a factor bound at one site influence a second gene elsewhere, tying separate loci into one circuit.

questions.explanation: Folding brings a distant regulatory site alongside the promoter, so a factor bound there can act on the machinery, and the effect weakens as the gap grows. The site need not sit next to the gene.
questions.hint: Think about how DNA can be folded.

questions.learningObjective: State what an acetyl tag does to DNA that is wrapped in proteins
questions.stem: The 2 August entry explains what an acetyl tag on the proteins around DNA does. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It loosens the hold the proteins have on the DNA, making the region easier for copying factors to reach.
It adds an acetyl group to the DNA bases, which changes the sequence of the gene.
options.misconception: claims the DNA bases are altered

options.text: It locks the DNA around the proteins more tightly, so the region becomes harder to read.
It adds a methyl group to the DNA instead, marking the gene for copying.

questions.explanation: An acetyl tag on the proteins around DNA weakens their grip and recruits proteins that help copying, so the region opens up. Claiming it alters the DNA bases is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the grip.

All three are needed for full activity, since two give far less than the complete set.
The factors act one after another, with each added factor giving the same extra activity.

questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that a silencing RNA pairs with DNA
questions.stem: The 3 February log claims that the small silencing RNA works because it pairs with the coding strand of the DNA and blocks the copying enzyme. Identify what is wrong with this claim.

options.text: The error is that silencing RNAs are always much longer than the messenger RNA they act on.
The error is that it pairs with the messenger RNA, not with the DNA, so it acts after copying.
The error is that small RNAs cannot recruit proteins at all.
The error is that the small RNA must be destroyed before it can act.
options.misconception: claims the RNA must be removed

questions.explanation: A silencing RNA pairs with the messenger RNA, usually through a protein complex, so it acts on the message after copying, not on the DNA. Blocking the copying enzyme is a different mechanism.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Mutation: A Change That Alters No Amino Acid
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a change that leaves the protein intact can still matter
questions.stem: The 19 September page asks whether a DNA change that leaves the protein untouched should be ignored. Explain why such a change can still matter to a cell.

answer.exemplar: Even when the protein sequence is unchanged, the base sequence of the message has changed, and the message is read by machinery that cares about its sequence in other ways. A change can alter how often the gene is copied, how efficiently the message is translated, how stable it is, or how well it is exported from the nucleus. Such changes can therefore have real effects on the cell, and they are also useful markers for tracing inherited variation through populations.

questions.explanation: The message sequence has still changed, and how a message is copied, translated and stabilised depends on it, so a silent change can matter. Calling it irrelevant overlooks those effects.
questions.hint: Think about what the message does besides code.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment separating a change in activity from a change in amount
questions.stem: The 13 February page asks how it could be shown that the rise in enzyme activity came from activation rather than from more enzyme. Describe the experiment.

answer.exemplar: Measure two things separately in the same tank cells: the amount of the enzyme, using an antibody or a calibrated gel, and the total product made per minute, which is the activity. Repeat both measurements before and after the treatment that raises the activity. If the amount of enzyme is unchanged while the product per minute rises, the change is in activity; if the enzyme amount rises as well, the change is in the amount, and a purification step can separate the two readings.

questions.explanation: Measuring the enzyme amount and the rate of product separately distinguishes activity from amount, and doing both before and after shows which moved. Rate alone tells little.
questions.hint: Measure amount and rate side by side.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: Where and Everywhere a Gene Is Read
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one gene is read in gills but not in muscle
questions.stem: The 4 January page asks why a gene can be read in the gills of a fish but not in its muscles. Explain how the same gene can be switched on in one tissue and off in another.

answer.exemplar: The gene and its regulatory DNA are identical in every cell, but each tissue carries its own set of regulatory proteins and its own chemical markings on the proteins around the DNA. In the gills the region around the gene is opened and the needed factors are present, so the gene is copied into messenger RNA, while in the muscle the region stays closed or a repressor is bound, so the same gene is not copied. The switch is therefore made by the environment of the tissue, not by a change in the gene itself.

questions.explanation: Every tissue has the same gene, but the regulatory proteins and DNA markings differ, so it is copied where conditions allow and quiet elsewhere. Claiming the gene differs between tissues is wrong.
questions.hint: Think about what each tissue carries.

answer.exemplar: Introduce the change into the tank cells, or work with a strain carrying it, and measure two things in parallel: the amount of the messenger RNA, by a reverse transcriptase reaction, and the amount of the protein, by an antibody assay, comparing both with cells that lack the change. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Needing Several Factors at Once
questions.learningObjective: Explain the advantage of a promoter needing several factors together
questions.stem: The 16 April page asks why a cell might build a promoter that cannot fire unless several factors are present together, rather than one that responds to a single factor. Explain the advantage of that arrangement.

answer.exemplar: A promoter that needs several factors only fires for the exact combination of conditions it was built for, so the cell can tell apart situations that would look the same if a single factor were enough. That matters in a crowded environment, where a signal such as a hormone might appear for many different reasons, and the cell must react to the right one. Several factors also let the response be graded and switched off again by removing one of them, which a single factor cannot do on its own.

questions.explanation: Requiring several factors lets the cell distinguish a particular combination of conditions from other situations sharing the same signal. Claiming a single factor is more reliable ignores that.
questions.hint: Think about telling situations apart.
